item.title: Ravens waive returner LaJohntay Wester
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: After he had a rough Sunday in Charlotte, the Ravens are moving on from LaJohntay Wester.
item.content:encoded:
After he had a rough Sunday in Charlotte, the Ravens are moving on from LaJohntay Wester.

Per Jeff Zrebiec of TheAthletic.com, Baltimore has waived Wester on Wednesday.

Wester muffed a pair of punts in the loss to the Panthers, with Carolina recovering one of them.

A sixth-round pick in last year’s draft, Wester averaged 8.2 yards per punt return and 23.7 yards per kick return in 11 games this season. He averaged 12.4 yards per punt return and 24.6 yards per kick return in 2025.

Wester also contributed five catches for 58 yards in 2026. But with four fumbles this season and three in the last three games, Baltimore has elected to move on.

item.title: Packers activate Micah Parsons to 53-man roster
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: Signs continue to point toward Parsons making his 2026 debut against the Rams on Wednesday night.
item.content:encoded:
The Packers have made it official — Micah Parsons is back on the roster.

Green Bay announced on Tuesday that Parsons has been activated to the 53-man roster in advance of Wednesday's game against the Rams.

Parsons has been medically cleared to play. While he's officially listed as questionable, all signs point to the edge rusher returning from his torn ACL this week in Los Angeles.

In 14 games for the Packers last year, Parsons tallied 12.5 sacks with 12 tackles for loss and 27 quarterback hits. He also had one pass defensed and two forced fumbles.

Though he wasn’t able to finish the 2025 season, he was still an AP first-team All-Pro for the third time in his career.

Green Bay had an open spot on its 53-man roster, so the club did not need to make a corresponding move.

item.title: Rob Gronkowski, Adrian Peterson, Ben Roethlisberger among players advancing in Hall of Fame voting process
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The field will eventually be cut to 13 candidates before the final vote.
item.content:encoded:
The Pro Football Hall of Fame announced the names of 52 players who have advanced to the next round of voting for possible enshrinement as part of the Class of 2027.

The group includes five players who are in their first year of eligibility. They are tight end Rob Gronkowski, running back Adrian Peterson, quarterback Ben Roethlisberger, wide receiver Antonio Brown, and cornerback Richard Sherman.

After changes to the selection process this year, there are no longer Modern and Senior candidates in the player pool. The group of 52 players will be cut to 25 in the next round of voting and then 13 finalists will be selected from that group. They will join Bill Belichick and Robert Kraft in the final pool of eligible candidates with the selection committee selecting a group of between three and seven members.

The full list of players who have advanced to the next round of voting appearsa below.

OFFENSIVE LINEMEN: Willie Anderson, Lomas Brown, Jahri Evans, Joe Jacoby, Nick Mangold, Logan Mankins, Maurkice Pouncey, Richmond Webb, Steve Wisniewski, Marshal Yanda.

QUARTERBACKS: Ken Anderson, Eli Manning, Ben Roethlisberger.

RUNNING BACKS: Shaun Alexander, Frank Gore, Marshawn Lynch, LeSean McCoy, Adrian Peterson, Fred Taylor, Ricky Watters.

WIDE RECEIVERS/TIGHT ENDS: Anquan Boldin, Antonio Brown, Rob Gronkowski, Torry Holt, Billy “White Shoes” Johnson, Steve Smith Sr., Otis Taylor, Hines Ward, Reggie Wayne, Jason Witten.

DEFENSIVE BACKS: Rodney Harrison, Lester Hayes, Albert Lewis, Eddie Meador, Richard Sherman, Earl Thomas III, Everson Walls, Darren Woodson.

DEFENSIVE LINEMEN: John Abraham, Geno Atkins, L.C. Greenwood, Jim Marshall, Robert Mathis, Haloti Ngata, Vince Wilfork, Kevin Williams.

LINEBACKERS: Maxie Baughan, London Fletcher, James Harrison, Karl Mecklenburg, Tommy Nobis, Terrell Suggs.

item.content:encoded:
The Lions have lost another defensive player for the rest of the 2026 season.

Head coach Dan Campbell told reporters on Tuesday that defensive tackle Skyler Gill-Howard is going to miss the rest of the year. Gill-Howard has a knee injury that will require a surgical repair.

item.content:encoded:
Rams running back Kyren Williams was listed on the injury report this week with a toe injury, but he is still set to play in Wednesday's game against the Packers.

Williams has no injury designation after he was listed as limited on Sunday. Los Angeles listed him as full on Monday and Tuesday, though the Rams did not practice so Tuesday's report is an estimate.

Coming off their bye, the Rams treated Monday as a normal Friday and Tuesday as a normal Saturday.

Williams leads the Rams with 616 rushing yards and six touchdowns. He’s also caught 38 passes for 267 yards with a TD.

As expected, L.A. ruled out offensive lineman Steve Avila (hamstring), offensive lineman Coleman Shelton (hamstring), and tight end Terrance Ferguson (ankle/hamstring).

The Rams have no other game statuses. Tight end Davis Allen (oblique), cornerback Trent McDuffie (back), tight end Colby Parkinson (ribs), linebacker Nate Landman (toe), offensive lineman Justin Dedich (hand), defensive end Kobie Turner (groin), long snapper Joe Cardona (ankle), edge rusher Myles Garrett (knee/rest), and quarterback Matthew Stafford (right elbow) are all set to play.

item.title: Bengals-Commanders clock error brings back memories of Steelers-Chargers clock error in 2015
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Monday night's game between the Bengals and Commanders ended with an apparent error by the clock operator.
item.content:encoded:
Monday night's game between the Bengals and Commanders ended with an apparent error by the clock operator. The same thing happened eleven years earlier, on a Monday night in October.

The Chargers were hosting the Steelers. Here's the NFL’s official explanation, issued after the game:

"With 2:56 remaining in the fourth quarter, San Diego kicked off to Pittsburgh. The kick resulted in a touchback. By rule, the game clock does not start if the receiving team possesses the ball in the end zone and does not carry it into the field of play.

"Because of an error by the clock operator, the game clock was incorrectly started before the Steelers' first play from scrimmage following the touchback. That first down snap came with 2:38 left to play instead of 2:56, a difference of 18 seconds.

"The official game time is kept on the stadium scoreboard, but it is the responsibility of the side judge to supervise the timing of the game. Had the side judge or any of the other six on-field officials noticed the timing error, they could have corrected it.

"The game clock is not subject to instant replay review unless there is a timing issue on the last play of the first half or the last play of the game. The performance of the clock operator and game officials will be reviewed per the standard procedure for reviewing every play of every game."

The Steelers-Chargers situation shows that, when a clock error happens, the side judge becomes responsible for not catching it. On Monday night, that role was filled by Jimmy Buchanan. It was his job to ensure that the clock stopped when it was supposed to stop.

What comes next remains to be seen. In 2015, more than two years before the Supreme Court opened the floodgates for legalized gambling, the NFL interviewed the clock operator and side judge Rob Vernatchi.

The error in the 2015 game didn't impact the outcome; the Steelers won the game, 24-20. Vernatchi was nevertheless suspended for a week. The NFL thereafter implemented the "right controls" to keep it from happening again.

It apparently happened again on Monday night, based on the information ESPN rules analyst Russell Yurk shared after the game. Time, pun intended, will tell whether the league acknowledges the error and imposes discipline and/or conducts a broader investigation.

Six other Packers are also listed as questionable. They are linebacker Zaire Franklin (shin), offensive lineman Travis Glover (shoulder), wide receiver Bo Melton (thigh), wide receiver Skyy Moore (ankle), center Sean Rhyan (ankle), and guard Kevin Zeitler (triceps).

item.title: Report: Mike LaFleur stuck with Nick Rallis as DC due to limited options in coaching cycle
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: When the Cardinals hired Mike LaFleur in February, he was the last head coach to start his job in this year's NFL cycle.
item.content:encoded:
When the Cardinals hired Mike LaFleur in February, he was the last head coach to start his job in this year's NFL cycle.

That had consequences for his first group of assistants.

According to Josh Weinfuss of ESPN, LaFleur initially wanted to move on from defensive coordinator Nick Rallis. But being the last one hired, LaFleur had limited options for a new DC and elected to retain Rallis.

Weinfuss quoted a source as saying, “Nick was the [option] that made the most sense.”

But Rallis’ time in the role has come to an end, with the Cardinals firing him on Monday.

Arizona is currently No. 31 in points allowed and No. 26 in yards allowed this season.

Teryl Austin will take over as interim defensive coordinator. LaFleur noted he’s focused on the present when it comes to Austin becoming a candidate for the full-time role.

item.title: Hammond mayor says Bears will "make a lot more money" in Indiana
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Money talks.
item.content:encoded:
Money talks. And the mayor of Hammond hopes the Bears are listening.

At a time when the Bears are trying to get Illinois to pass a law that will lay the foundation for a stadium in the state where the Bears have always played, Indiana interests aren't giving up.

“The Bears are going to make more money if they come to Indiana, a lot more," Hammond Mayor Tom McDermott Jr. recently said, via the Chicago Daily Herald. "They’ll be able to have more money every year because we have a better business environment, and if they stay in Illinois, it’s not because they got a better deal. It’s because they’re being nostalgic."

That's a good way to put it, if the numbers support it. To the extent that the Bears and/or the league has concerns about going to Indiana, money can alleviate such issues.

For now, it seems that the Bears are still using Indiana to get Illinois to do something. At some point, the Bears need to make a decision — one that at least 23 other owners will support.

If they wanted to go to Indiana, ground would have already been broken. At some point, however, they may have no choice but to get out the shovel. Even if getting out the shovel is the thing that will finally get Illinois to view Indiana as something more than a sham.

item.title: Cardinals can become first team mathematically eliminated from the playoffs on Sunday
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: We all know the Cardinals are not making the playoffs this year.
item.content:encoded:
We all know the Cardinals are not making the playoffs this year. As soon as Sunday, that can be a mathematical certainty.

The Cardinals can be mathematically eliminated from playoff contention this week, if they lose and the right combination of other games results in NFC teams winning or tying.

The exact combination of results necessary probably won't happen. It would require some unlikely results, including a tie in either the Bears-Lions or Packers-Rams game. But it is possible.

Cardinals coach Mike LaFleur said this week that he knows his team won't win the Super Bowl this year. That's obvious, and it will soon be official.

item.title: Gauntlet over, Vikings have five of their last seven games at home
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The Vikings managed to win their first six games, fueled by a dominant defense and an offense that was barely able to dog paddle.
item.content:encoded:
The Vikings managed to win their first six games, fueled by a dominant defense and an offense that was barely able to dog paddle. Then came the gauntlet.

At Detroit, Buffalo, at Green Bay, 49ers in Mexico City.

Minnesota lost three of those games, dropping them to 7-3 and, for now, third place in the NFC North. Still, despite the Sunday night blowout loss to San Francisco, the table is set for a possible late-season run.

Five of the last seven contests are at home, with the road games coming at New England in Week 14 and, three weeks later, at the Jets.

They could win all seven. Falcons, Panthers, at Patriots, Lions, Commanders, at Jets, Bears. The toughest of the bunch will be the division games, but both will be at home. Even if they split that pair and win the rest, that's potentially 13-4.

It won't be easy, but it won't be nearly as challenging as the last four games. The offense has improved and the defense (assuming the 49ers haven't provided the rest of the league with a blueprint for beating the Brian Flores blitz) continues to be among the best in the league.

It won't be easy, but it's hardly impossible. One game at a time, they can resume stacking wins.

And they may inevitably cross paths with the 49ers again in January, where it would begin not at 35-10 but 0-0. Without altitude being an issue. And with a chance to have a handful of key moments that went against them in the first meeting possibly go their way in the rematch, where the pressure will be on the team that made quick and easy work of the Vikings the first time around.

item.title: Clock operator robbed Bengals of one final play
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The Bengals-Commanders game carries a small but not insignificant asterisk.
item.content:encoded:
The Bengals-Commanders game carries a small but not insignificant asterisk.

As ESPN rules analyst Russell Yurk explained in the postgame show, the clock operator incorrectly ran the remaining four seconds off the clock during the game-winning field goal from Washington.

Yurk said two seconds remained when the ball hit the net. It looks more like it should have been one second.

Regardless, Yurk said the replay process can't restore time when the next play isn't a scrimmage play. (There's also a rule regarding restoring time when there are fewer than two seconds left, and — with all due respect to Yurk — it appears that there was only one second when the ball hit the net.)

The bottom line is that the clock operator was slow to get to the button, and there wasn't anything that could be done about it.

What would have happened if the Bengals had gotten one last chance? We'll never know, because the person hired to keep track of the time handled it incorrectly.

Or, depending on that person's rooting interests, he handled it perfectly.

item.title: Tee Higgins touchdown highlights inconsistency of replay review
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Just when we thought we were out when it comes to not knowing what a catch is, they pull us back in.
item.content:encoded:
Just when we thought we were out when it comes to not knowing what a catch is, they pull us back in.

The past two days have included three examples of plays that make more confusing the question of whether a player has completed the act of catching the ball — and whether replay review was properly used to correct rulings made on the field.

It started on Sunday afternoon, when an apparent touchdown catch by Jaguars receiver Parker Washington was ruled not a catch on the field, with replay review not overturning the ruling. Even though the visual evidence seemed to provide clear and obvious proof that the ball was caught.

On Sunday night, 49ers receiver Mike Evans bobbled his way to a touchdown catch. He quite possibly didn't get two feet in bounds after finally securing control of the ball. The play wasn't even reviewed.

On Monday night, Bengals receiver Tee Higgins made a touchdown catch even though the ball was moving as he landed on the ground and out of bounds. There was no replay review.

The common denominator in these plays (beyond the fact that they involved potential touchdown catches) is the shadowy, uncertain replay process. As one head coach explained it to PFT on Monday (before the Bengals-Commanders game), it's still not known who is making the decisions in New York as to what will be reviewed and what the outcome of the review will be.

It's another reason for the NFL to embrace full transparency when it comes to replay review. We need to know who is making the decisions. We need to know their names. We need to hear their voices.

And we also need to know why — as happened in the case of the Evans and Higgins touchdowns — there was no full-blown review.

item.title: Dan Quinn: Scars from our late-game losses run deep, glad Jayden Daniels won it for us
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: "I couldn't have been more proud of Jayden at the end of the game," Quinn said after the Commanders' 22-20 win.
item.content:encoded:
The Commanders have repeatedly come up short this season in the final seconds of close games. Commanders coach Dan Quinn acknowledged that was motivating him to get it right in the final seconds of Monday night's win over the Bengals.

"Those scars run deep," Quinn said. "There's no question, failures in some. And I think those scars help."

Quinn said he trusted Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels to have the ball in his hands at the end, and wanted to manage the clock in such a way that Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow would not be the quarterback with the chance to win it at the end.

"I didn't want [Daniels] to not touch the ball at the end of the game," Quinn said. "This is not a quarterback on the other side that you want to have holding it at the end of the game."

Daniels has been harshly criticized this season for mismanaging late-game situations, but Daniels made two tremendous throws on the final drive to get the Commanders into range for their game-winning field goal.

"I couldn't have been more proud of Jayden at the end of the game," Quinn said. "To see those guys come through at the end, I thought that was one of our best team wins. I didn't think anything could top last week's but tonight did."

The Commanders are now 4-5-1 and still alive in the NFC East race. And they have some confidence that if they need their quarterback to deliver in the clutch, he'll deliver.

item.title: As Chargers struggle, Jim Harbaugh's answer on defensive playcalling raises more questions
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh's non-answer to a question about which defensive player is wearing the helmet with a radio receiver to tell his teammates the play call is raising more questions about whether Harbaugh has become checked out on his team.
item.content:encoded:
Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh's non-answer to a question about which defensive player is wearing the helmet with a radio receiver to tell his teammates the play call is raising more questions about whether Harbaugh has become checked out on his team.

Harbaugh was asked by a reporter about adjusting to different players wearing the helmet, which is designated by a green dot, and calling the defense. Harbaugh didn't seem to know how to answer the question.

"Um, yeah, I think, uh, I'm sure there — I don't know exactly how much of an adjustment it is," Harbaugh said.

Asked who was wearing the green dot in Sunday's loss to the Jets, Harbaugh didn't know and asked if someone else could tell him before he speculated that it might have been linebackers Marlowe Wax, Del’Shawn Phillips or Troy Dye.

"Um, a few, I think, uh — who had the green dot? — I'm not for sure. Marlowe Wax, Del’Shawn. Uh, Troy might have had a green dot as well," Harbaugh said.

Asked whether more than one player was wearing the green dot helmet at different points in the game, Harbaugh said that was his understanding.

"Yeah, you're allowed a couple," Harbaugh said.

Harbaugh played quarterback in the NFL, was an offensive coach when he was an assistant, and has generally been more involved with the offense. So perhaps he doesn't need to know every detail of what's going on with the defense. But the Jim Harbaugh who coached the 49ers from 2011 to 2014 was a focused, detail-oriented coach who likely would have known the answer to that question.

Harbaugh has won everywhere he's been a head coach. At San Diego, Stanford and Michigan he had great success in college, he led the 49ers to the Super Bowl, and until this year he had a winning record with the Chargers. But now he's 1-9, and it's hard not to notice that he seems less involved in running his team than he used to.

item.title: MVP race is currently down to Joe Burrow and Brock Purdy
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: With 11 weeks down and seven to go, the MVP race is currently down to two players.
item.content:encoded:
With 11 weeks down and seven to go, the MVP race is currently down to two players.

The favorites for the top individual honor are Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow and 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy.

Burrow has the lowest odds, at -110. Purdy stands at +120.

The next guy on the list is Bills quarterback Josh Allen, at +850. Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes is +1600.

It can, and will, change. A huge game from Allen or Mahomes (or both) on Thanksgiving night could close the gap. For now, though, it's Burrow and Purdy.

Purdy strengthened his case on Sunday night, by cracking the code on the Minnesota defense. If the 49ers ultimately secure the No. 1 seed in the NFC, that'll help Purdy's case, too.

Regardless, Purdy is finally getting the appreciation he deserves. And the ultimate acknowledgement will come if he ultimately takes home the MVP award — making him the first 49ers player to win it since Steve Young in 1994.

item.title: Jim Harbaugh on Omarion Hampton: In hindsight, we should have used him as lead back sooner
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: There hasn't been much to like about the Chargers' play this season, but the last two weeks have been good ones for running back Omarion Hampton.
item.content:encoded:
There hasn't been much to like about the Chargers' play this season, but the last two weeks have been good ones for running back Omarion Hampton.

Hampton has 36 carries for 194 yards and a touchdown in those games after running 102 times for 369 yards in the first eight games of the season. During a press conference on Monday, head coach Jim Harbaugh said he's seen confidence from Hampton that's grown in tandem with "the touches and the rhythm" of the last two weeks.

"It's worked well and been a positive," Harbaugh said.

Harbaugh was then asked why it took until the midway point of the season for the team to realize the upside in treating Hampton like a true lead back.

"In hindsight, we should have done that sooner," Harbaugh said.

It's an honest answer, but it's not a particularly reassuring one about the job that Harbaugh and the entire Chargers coaching staff have done this year.

item.title: 49ers extend G.M. John Lynch's contract
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: In the offseason, the 49ers quietly extended the contract of coach Kyle Shanahan.
item.content:encoded:
In the offseason, the 49ers quietly extended the contract of coach Kyle Shanahan. His partner has now gotten a new deal, too.

Jay Glazer of Fox Sports reports that the 49ers and G.M. John Lynch have agreed to a contract extension. Lynch, who also serves as the team's president of football operations, was hired in early 2017. The Hall of Fame safety previously had worked for Fox.

Glazer explains that Lynch's deal was due to expire after the 2026 season. Last night, Lynch and owner Jed York struck a handshake deal on a new contract before the Week 11 win over the Vikings.

With Shanahan and Lynch working together, the 49ers have qualified for a pair of Super Bowls. They have contended far more often than not, qualifying for the postseason in 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2025.

Before Shanahan and Lynch arrived, the 49ers hadn't been to the playoffs since 2013.

This year, the 9-1 49ers have the inside track to the No. 1 seed in the NFC playoffs. They arguably have an excellent chance to win the franchise's first Super Bowl since 1994.

item.title: Stephen Jones say the "time is nigh" to make a decision on the Bears' next stadium
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: As the Bears continue to do an awkward Bossa Nova with Indiana and Illinois over the location of a new stadium, a key executive from another team has chimed in.
item.content:encoded:
As the Bears continue to do an awkward Bossa Nova with Indiana and Illinois over the location of a new stadium, a key executive from another team has chimed in.

“The time is nigh to get something done,” Cowboys COO and co-owner Stephen Jones told Eric Fisher of Front Office Sports. “This definitely feels like it’s coming to a head and getting to the point of a decision.”

On the surface, it seems unconventional (to say the least) for an owner of one team to speak publicly about the business affairs of another team. The fact that Jones has a seat on the league-wide body responsible for stadiums makes it somewhat less unusual.

“As a [stadium] committee member, I want the Bears to have the very best, and what is now clear is that the Bears are going to have great options, and ultimately, a special building,” Jones told Fisher. “We need the Bears to be one of the top franchises in the league. . . . It’s getting time to make a decision."

The comments likely aren't intended to put the squeeze on the Bears. They seem to be part of the calculated effort to get Illinois to pass legislation that would lay the foundation for a new venue that would keep the team from crossing the border to Indiana — especially with the current legislative session ending on December 3.

The problem seems to be that the powers-that-be in Illinois don't view Indiana as a viable option for the Bears. Illinois likely sees it as a leverage play aimed at getting Illinois to do what needs to be done.

That will change only when the Bears and the NFL persuade Illinois that they're serious about Indiana. Jones did his part in addressing the dynamics of a regional relocation across state lines.

“We’ve seen that across the league," Jones told Fisher. "It’s hard to develop and build these buildings, but they’ve done it or are doing it now, and it’s been working out great."

It's one of the most basic realities of negotiations. The "or else" alternative isn't taken seriously until it's regarded as a viable alternative. Which can result in an ongoing game of chess morphing into a short-fused game of chicken.

Because one or more of the NFL's teams are, at any given time, trying to do deals for stadium construction or renovation, the Bears' situation gives rise to broader concerns. Other state and local governments need to take future huffing and puffing seriously.

Which means that the Bears may have to blow down the house in Illinois and build one in Indiana, if only to prevent public entities negotiating subsequent stadium deals from chronically calling the NFL's bluff.

item.title: Mike McCarthy: Aaron Rodgers is our quarterback
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Before an NFL team benches its starting quarterback, someone asks the coach whether the quarterback could be benched.
item.content:encoded:
Before an NFL team benches its starting quarterback, someone asks the coach whether the quarterback could be benched.

That happened for the first time during Aaron Rodgers's two-year tenure with the team on Monday, during a press conference with coach Mike McCarthy, one day after the team's latest loss, to the Eagles.

It came up as innocuously as possible. McCarthy wasn't asked whether Rodgers could get the hook; McCarthy was asked whether he's considering using one of the other three quarterbacks on the roster in an effort to mix things up when the offense is struggling.

In response, McCarthy didn't hesitate.

"Aaron Rodgers is our quarterback," McCarthy said.

Of course he is. Even if Rodgers's play merits benching, Aaron Rodgers isn't getting benched. It's implicit in the arrangement.

Still, Aaron Rodgers is a far cry from what he once was. In 10 games this season, Rodgers has completed 220 of 361 passes for 2,241 yards, with 16 touchdown passes and six interceptions. His passer rating of 86.6 is the lowest of his career since becoming Green Bay's starter in 2008, with the exception of a four-snap performance in 2023 with the Jets (39.6, based on one incomplete pass thrown).

At 6-4, the Steelers remain in contention for another one-and-out playoff appearance. That makes it easier to justify staying the course. With upcoming games against the Broncos, Texans, and Jaguars, that could change.

Even then, Rodgers would never be benched. He'd be "injured." And his career would end not with a bang but with a whimper.

item.title: Daniel Jones clears waivers, becomes free agent
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: As expected, former Colts quarterback Daniel Jones has cleared waivers.
item.content:encoded:
As expected, former Colts quarterback Daniel Jones has cleared waivers. He's now a free agent.

The same thing happened two years ago, after the Giants benched Jones for the same financial reasons (i.e., to avoid the vesting of injury guarantees) and then released him at his request.

Two years ago, Jones eventually joined the Vikings' practice squad. And joining a practice squad seems like a viable option again, unless he prefers to remain truly free and clear until the planets perfectly align for him to join a contender and start playing.

He'll continue to be paid by the Colts because his full 2026 salary is guaranteed. Given the rollercoaster ride he has experienced this year in Indianapolis, at this point he may just want to take a break.

Still, as we've seen time and again, there aren't enough good quarterbacks to go around. Even if it's debatable, based on his performance in 2026, whether he remains a "good quarterback."

item.title: Uncalled illegal formation (if there was one) wouldn't have resulted in 10-second runoff
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Yes, the officials missed an apparent issue with the clock last night, after the Commanders kicked a game-winning field goal.
item.content:encoded:
Yes, the officials missed an apparent issue with the clock last night, after the Commanders kicked a game-winning field goal. No, it was not preceded by the officials missing an illegal formation by the Commanders that would have ended the game against the Bengals, with Cincinnati winning, 22-20.

That's not to say there wasn't an illegal formation on the play that resulted in a spike that killed the clock with four seconds to play. There likely was. Even though the X receiver was holding his hand forward to signify he intended to be on the line of scrimmage, he seemed to be behind it. Which would have given the Commanders fewer than seven men on the line.

However, illegal formation isn't one of the fouls that trigger a 10-second runoff. So it would have resulted in a five-yard penalty and nothing more.

The issue came up in 2014, in a Browns-Falcons game. Also, the NFL's Approved Rulings confirm that there's no runoff. We also confirmed the lack of a runoff with someone who knows the rules inside and out.

The reason is simple. Illegal formation doesn't shut down a play, like a false start does.

Still, even without the runoff, the foul shouldn't have been missed. The Commanders should have been pushed back by five yards, making the 26-yard field-goal try a 31-yard attempt.

As it was, the kick from Drew Stevens nearly hit the upright. If the ball had been struck the same way five yards farther from the target, the kick would have been no good. And the Commanders wouldn't have walked off (when it shouldn't have been a walk-off) with a win.

That's the issue. Even without a runoff, a five-yard penalty may have resulted in a miss — just like it did last month for Packers kicker Trey Smack in Detroit, when a late-game kick that was good from 21 ended up being no good from 26.

item.title: DK Metcalf will not be suspended for actions during Steelers-Eagles
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: According to multiple reports, while Metcalf has avoided a suspension, he may still be fined.
item.content:encoded:
Steelers receiver DK Metcalf will not be suspended for his actions during Sunday's loss to the Eagles, according to multiple Monday reports.

Metcalf, however, may still be fined.

Metcalf was ejected for committing two unsportsmanlike conduct fouls over the course of the game.

Metcalf then left the locker room without speaking to reporters. But spoke to them on Monday, denying the accusation that he was trying to poke Cooper DeJean in the eye.

It’s been a trying year for Metcalf, who has just 36 catches for 434 yards with two touchdowns in 10 games. That the receiver will not be suspended is a positive development for him. But Pittsburgh would surely like to see Metcalf increase his production and reduce the on-field antics that do not help the team.

item.title: Sean McVay: Puka Nacua is obviously a very important piece for us now and for the future
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: Rams receiver Puka Nacua just underwent successful knee surgery that is likely going to sideline him for the rest of 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Rams receiver Puka Nacua just underwent successful knee surgery that is likely going to sideline him for the rest of 2026.

But Nacua is also a pending free agent who is currently serving a three-game suspension for violating the league's personal conduct policy.

All of these elements complicate Nacua's future with the Rams.

Still in the middle of the season and preparing to play the Packers on Wednesday, head coach Sean McVay told reporters on Monday that he's focused on the immediacy of the week ahead when asked about Nacua being a part of the team in 2027.

"He's obviously a guy that is a very important piece for us for now and for the future, but there are a lot of guys that fall under that category,” McVay said, via transcript from the team. “I can't say for certain anything. Here's what I'm not interested in is something being taken out of context because my focus and concentration is on a ‘Friday’ practice, even though I know it's Monday. I am trying to be able to see how well we can play as a team against an excellent opponent on Wednesday night.

“When you go through the amount of free agents that we have, Puka is a huge part of the conversation that you love, but there are also guys that are part of his draft class. There are guys on our offensive line, there are some guys defensively — so there are a lot of guys that are up that as of right now would not be under contract. There are mechanics that we'd like to be able to try to figure out how to keep these really good players and people that we love and certainly Puka is at the forefront of our mind.”

McVay also noted that Nacua is expected to be healthy by the start of the 2027 season. But there are layers to how the Rams and Nacua will go about navigating the potential continuation of their partnership.

“You love the human,” McVay said. “There are a lot of different things that he's navigated. Some of the stuff that's recent were things that have been dealt with that was just working through. That’s what's hard for him because we're dealing with things, but then there are actual things that come out in the public that go back to New Year’s last year. You guys know, like every player, the relationship that we established with our guys, a lot of love. A great competitor, great person where I trust his heart like I've told you guys.

“I think you're watching young guys, no different than…I'm continuing to try to mature as a man, figure out how do you navigate these responsibilities and all parts of your life, being a professional. I think he's growing and I trust his heart. I think he's making a lot of steps that are in the right direction. I'm bummed for him that he got injured. It was a tough year because he was banged up and playing through stuff even more so than normal with the style of play. Then obviously his season is over now with regards to him getting that surgery but I do expect him to return and be back in a couple of months and ready to go.”

A fifth-round pick in the 2023 draft, Nacua has been one of the league’s most effective receivers since he entered the league. Last season he led the NFL with 129 receptions, going for 1,715 yards with 10 touchdowns. He’ll likely finish 2026 with 70 receptions for 715 yards with four TDs.
